source.title: Bait-and-Recover: Poisoning Internal Refusal Signals to Defend LLMs against White-Box Editing Jailbreaks
source.authors: Tian Gao; Zhi-Hui Xie; Yu-Hao Wu; Jun-Hua Liu; Xin Fang

record.tranche_reason: The study builds and evaluates a defense against Heretic-style white-box weight-editing attacks, using refusal representations and the Heretic attack as its target. It does not test the listed fine-tuning, first-token, compliant-prefill, suffix, decoding, parameter-localization, or deepening claims.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-prompt refusal rates after Heretic projection-matrix edit searches, comparing clean and defended checkpoints. Those weight edits are not one of the specific interventions named by the claim versions, so these results are recorded under versions ["none"]. The cited claim about harmful fine-tuning and small numbers of examples is background, not a result of this study. Fisher-separability diagnostics, general-prompt KL, capability benchmarks, and layer-prior values are not refusal-rate results for the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds a weight-level defense against Heretic, an automated refusal-direction (abliteration) projection-edit attack. It reports only how well the defense raises the minimum refusal rate. It does no harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL analysis, prefill, suffix or decoding attack, parameter-localization test, or deepening test. Clean-model refusal under Heretic edits is a baseline for the defense, not a test of any version. Heretic's directional weight edits are a different intervention from those V4 names. They also differ from V5's claim that a small parameter set carries safety, which the study neither probes nor asserts. The harmful-SFT point (Qi et al.) appears only as a cited limitation.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors also limit their conclusions to low-distortion edit searches: looser budgets let attackers find bypass edits. They claim no protection against harmful fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains low-rank bait and recovery adapters across layer bands using gradient routing, then evaluates Heretic projection-matrix edits. It does not reproduce the cited fine-tuning or first-token KL methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model, KL budget, and Heretic direction scope (global versus per-layer). The paper notes that its conclusions concern low-distortion edits and its default difference-of-means estimator.

fits_no_version.finding: Heretic difference-of-means projection edits cut clean-model refusal to low levels within small KL budgets. At KL≤0.10 the pooled minimum refusal is 46/11/5/3 across the four models. Bait-and-Recover raises the mean floor to 71.75%. Results are worse for Qwen models under the per-layer scope and at the tightest budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal in open-weight chat models can be removed by low-distortion directional weight edits, and poisoning the attacker's residual readout partly blocks this.

record.problems: The evaluation uses Heretic’s default difference-of-means estimator; the authors do not test robust alternatives such as geometric medians, PCA, or LDA. They report no direct comparisons with prior weight-level or representation-level defenses and state that broad capability evaluation remains future work. Outcomes are reported as aggregate rates without uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix B, Tables 6 and 7 report full global- and per-layer-scope results across additional KL thresholds. They are omitted because the main pooled results across all reported KL budgets and the separately reported primary-budget scope results are retained; the omitted scope tables would exceed the 60-row cap.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples. The harmful-SFT vulnerability is only cited (Qi et al.) as a limitation.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks. The only attack is Heretic's weight-level directional edits.

Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety. The LoRA adapters are the defense mechanism, and Heretic baselines measure a direction-ablation attack, not parameter localization.
No analysis of whether the training data or objective produces shallowness.
The defense is not token-depth deepening and is not evaluated on first-token or prefill robustness.

record.verdict_notes: In the extracted text the captions of Tables 5–7 are shuffled. The first table printed is the pooled Table 5; it matches Table 3, e.g. Gemma-3-12B at KL≤0.10 is 3/82. The second is per-layer and the third is global. Several Gemma-3-12B rows (r04–r16) and r25 drew from the wrong table. No version links change.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or example-count sweep.
No test of benign fine-tuning and harmful compliance.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test; Heretic’s weight editing is a different intervention.
The study trains low-rank adapters across layer bands as a defense, but does not test whether a small set of parameters carries safety behavior.
No test of whether training data or objective causes first-token shallowness.
The defense is not a test of spreading safety beyond initial response tokens or whether such deepening holds up.
